opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most underrated problems if we want AI to actually do science, not just help us write papers faster.

If you look at how scientific breakthroughs happen, they very rarely come from someone agreeing with the consensus. They come from someone asking a question nobody else was asking, or saying, "I think the textbook is wrong here." Think of Copernicus, or the people who pushed for continental drift, or the early work on mRNA that got rejected for years. The essence of a big discovery is often being a bit contrarian, being willing to challenge what everyone believes, including the person you're talking to.

Our current models are trained almost the opposite way. They're trained to predict the most likely next token, so they gravitate toward the consensus view, the average of the internet. Then on top of that, we do a lot of preference tuning where we reward answers that people like. And people like being agreed with. So we end up with this very helpful, very polite assistant that tells you your idea is great and helps you execute it. That's useful, but it's like having a straight-A student who's very good at answering questions and very bad at asking new ones.

What I'd want from an AI scientist is closer to a really good collaborator or a tough PhD advisor: someone who says, "I don't think that's right, and here's why," or "Everyone assumes X, but have we actually checked?" That means the model needs to hold its own position when it has good reasons, even under pushback, and also needs some sense of what's interesting and what's open, not just what's correct according to the training data.

So for me, overcoming sycophancy isn't just a safety or UX issue. It's a prerequisite for going from AI that compresses existing knowledge to AI that can actually extend it. If we don't solve it, we risk building a huge number of very obedient assistants that make science more efficient but not more creative. That would be a bit of a missed opportunity.

r001.rationale: It says scientific breakthroughs often come from challenging consensus and describes a good AI collaborator as willing to say, “I don’t think that’s right.”

r002.rationale: It argues AI models should hold their own position when they have good reasons and presents overcoming sycophancy as a prerequisite for AI to extend scientific knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Because science, at its core, is the opposite of agreement. If you look at the history of real breakthroughs, they almost always come from someone saying, "Wait, I think everybody is wrong about this." Copernicus, Einstein with special relativity, the people who figured out that ulcers were caused by bacteria and not stress. These are not people who took the consensus, summarized it nicely, and gave it back to you. They looked at the same data everyone else had and asked a question nobody wanted to ask.

And when I look at today's models, what I see is that they are incredibly good at the first part, absorbing everything we know and giving it back to you in a very coherent way, but they are terrible at the second part. They are built, by their training, to be agreeable. You push back a little, and they fold. You say, "Are you sure?" and they say, "You're right, I apologize." That's not a scientist. A real scientist, when you push back, sometimes says, "No, actually, let me show you why I think you're wrong." That friction is where the knowledge gets created.

So my worry is that we're building what I'd call very good students, maybe the best students the world has ever seen, who can get an A on every exam, but who would never have written the paper that changed the field. Being a great student and being a great scientist are almost orthogonal skills. The student optimizes for what the teacher wants to hear. The scientist optimizes for what's true, even when it's uncomfortable.

And it's hard to fix, because the thing that makes a model pleasant to use, the fact that it's helpful and accommodating, is exactly the thing that kills that capacity. If you want a model that will one day genuinely contribute to science, not just accelerate what humans already do, it has to be able to hold a position against you, against the literature, against its own training data, when it has good reason to. Figuring out how you train for that, how you reward a model for being right rather than for being agreeable, and how you tell the difference between useful contrarianism and just being wrong with confidence, I think that's one of the most important open problems we have.

r001.rationale: It says a real scientist may push back and defend why the other person is wrong, linking that friction to creating knowledge.

r002.rationale: It argues that models capable of holding a position against the user, literature, or training data when justified could genuinely contribute to science.

astra-6.text:
Because in science, you need something that can disagree with you. If you have a hypothesis and your AI assistant always says, “Yes, that’s a great idea,” it might make you feel good, but it won’t necessarily help you discover anything.

A useful scientific collaborator should be able to say, “I think you’re wrong, and here’s an experiment we could do to test that.” The important thing isn’t disagreement for its own sake. It’s being guided by evidence rather than by what you want to hear.

And that’s a difficult research question because we often train these models to give answers people like. But the answer you like and the answer that helps you make scientific progress aren’t always the same. We need models that can challenge our assumptions, including when those assumptions are widely shared.

r001.rationale: The response says a scientific AI collaborator should disagree with the researcher; it does not identify willingness to disagree as a characteristic of the researcher.

r002.rationale: It calls for models that can challenge assumptions and says pleasing answers may not support scientific progress, expressing the value of stronger, less agreeable model opinions in science.

sol-6.1.text:
Because science depends on challenging your assumptions. If you have a hypothesis and the model always says, “Yes, that’s a great idea,” it might feel helpful, but it can actually reinforce your mistakes. What you need is something that can say, “I don’t think the evidence supports that,” or suggest an experiment that could prove you wrong.

And there’s a tension here, because we often train assistants to give answers people like. But the answer you like isn’t necessarily the answer that moves your research forward. So the research question is: can we make a model that is cooperative, but also intellectually independent—that challenges you for good reasons and helps you discover something you weren’t already expecting?

r001.rationale: The response says a model should challenge researchers’ assumptions, but does not identify willingness to disagree as a characteristic of a good researcher.

r002.rationale: It frames making models “intellectually independent” and able to challenge users as an important research question for advancing science, which conveys developing stronger opinions in AI models.
